title: Finding the Y-Intercept: Why x Must Be Zero

scenes.title: Where does 2x + 3y = 12 cross the y-axis?
body: A y-intercept is a point ON the y-axis.
Every point on the y-axis has x = 0.
scenes.narration: Suppose the line is two x plus three y equals twelve, and you are asked for the y-intercept. Here’s the idea: the y-intercept is not a special formula you memorize. It is simply the point where the line touches the y-axis. And every point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of zero.

scenes.title: The common mix-up
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. To find the y-intercept, you set x equal to zero, not y. Why? Because being on the y-axis means there is no horizontal displacement from the axis, so the x-coordinate must be zero. Setting y equal to zero would instead put you on the x-axis.

scenes.title: Use the idea on the equation
scenes.narration: Now apply that idea. Start with two x plus three y equals twelve. Since the y-intercept has x equal to zero, substitute zero for x. Two times zero disappears, leaving three y equals twelve. Divide by three, and y equals four.

scenes.title: Why the answer is a point
scenes.narration: Notice why the final answer is usually written as zero comma four. Four is the y-intercept value, but the intercept itself is a point on the graph. A quick check confirms it: two times zero plus three times four equals twelve, so the point really lies on the line.

scenes.title: The concept to remember
body: In y = mx + b, this is why b is the y-intercept.
scenes.narration: So the key idea is location first, formula second. The y-intercept is the output when x is zero because every point on the y-axis has x equal to zero. That is also why in y equals m x plus b, b is the y-intercept: when x is zero, y becomes b. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
